tagline.text: A 2,700 m vegetable-terrace ridge beside Halsema Highway

location.label: Location
location.text: Cattubo, Atok, Benguet (near KM 55 of Halsema Highway)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–March dry season (sea of clouds mostly December–February)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to a full day (overnight for sunrise)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱400–1,200 (day trip from Baguio, covering round-trip bus, registration, guide and food)

children.text: A peak of about 2,717 m above sea level, reached by a concrete village road that branches off Halsema Highway in Atok, Benguet. Vegetable terraces and a Way of the Cross trail run almost to the top, so it is easy even for beginners, and on clear days it offers views of Mt. Pulag, the Kabayan valley and a sea of clouds at dawn.
Mt. Timbak sits in Barangay Cattubo, Atok, Benguet, and is also called Mt. Singakalsa. Many sources give its height as about
above sea level, while the Wikipedia list of Cordillera peaks shows about

. It is often described as the third highest mountain in Luzon, but the same list places it fourth, after Pulag, Tabayoc and Pual, so the ranking varies by source. Either way, given how easy it is to reach from Manila, it is one of the simplest ways to stand on a peak above 2,700 m.

The feel of the hike is very different from a typical jungle trek. A concrete village road branches off Halsema Highway near KM 55, passes Mongoto (Timbak) Elementary School and continues up the mountainside, lined with terraces of carrots, cabbage, celery and radish and with local homes. Near the top stand a small Calvary hill with three white crosses and Stations of the Cross markers, so the trail also serves as a pilgrimage route during Lent. Because the whole mountain is cleared farmland, this is less a forest climb than a highland walk between villages and fields.

The views are the main attraction. On a clear day you can see the ridges toward Mt. Pulag and Mt. Tabayoc, the Kabayan valley and the Kabayan–Abatan road below, and peaks on the Ifugao side, layered one behind another. At dawn a sea of clouds fills the valleys beneath you. On days when low cloud settles in, everything can turn white, so treat the view as a bonus that depends on the weather.

It also helps to understand the cultural background. Mt. Timbak is land the Ibaloi people have lived on for generations, and a burial cave on the mountainside once held ancestral mummies preserved with fire and smoke. Visits to the cave are reported to be suspended for conservation reasons, so think of this mountain as a place for scenery, not for seeing mummies. For more on mummy culture, see
Kabayan Mummy Caves
. After an overnight bus from Manila to Baguio, you can catch a bus toward Sagada or Bontoc and hike in a single day, and you can combine it with the flower farms of
Atok

and the former highest highway point on the same road. This guide draws on a handful of travel reports and Wikipedia, and registration rules, fees and trail conditions change often, so check the latest notices at the Atok municipal tourism office before you go.

Beside the roadside waiting shed at KM 55, a sign points to Mongoto Elementary School and the Timbak mummy cave, and the concrete road starts here. Take a bus from Baguio toward Sagada or Bontoc, tell the conductor "KM 55, please," and you will be dropped on the right side of the road.

Terraces of carrots, cabbage, celery and potatoes stretch almost to the summit. Since the road runs between fields, simply ask residents at the roadside houses whenever you wonder if you are on the right track. Do not step into the fields; stay on the concrete road and the field-edge paths.
Just below the summit, three white crosses and religious statues are visible from afar. During Lent this path is used for the Way of the Cross, so pass quietly if worshippers are praying.

blocks.title: Summit views and the radio tower

children.text: The summit is an open ridge of grass and fields with a communications tower nearby. On clear days you can see Mt. Pulag, Mt. Tabayoc, the Kabayan valley and the Ifugao peaks, and many reports say mobile signal is available along most of the trail.

blocks.title: Dawn sea of clouds and sunrise

children.text: The view is far better when clouds fill the valleys early in the morning. To catch the sunrise, you can stay overnight at a nearby homestay or campsite and climb in the early dawn. Night hiking is not recommended because you may trample the farmland.
The Timbak trail is part of a village road that continues to the Kabayan side. Reaching Kabayan means descending about
over a steep, long route that takes several hours, so you need a guide and should confirm local transport.

blocks.title: Former highest highway point and flower farms

children.text: A few minutes by car from KM 55 is Atok's former "highest point in the Philippine Highway System" viewpoint. Wikipedia says this spot in Barangay Paoay, at
above sea level, held that title until early 2019. Combined with the Northern Blossom Flower Farm, it makes a good half-day outing.

items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: By bus from Baguio and on foot

children.text: Board the first bus toward Sagada or Bontoc at the Dangwa terminal or the Slaughterhouse terminal on Magsaysay Avenue in Baguio. The day is long, so the earliest bus is best; check the last return bus ahead of time.
Get off at the roadside waiting shed at KM 55, stock up on snacks and water, and check the signs. The ride takes around
2–3 hours
depending on traffic.
Walk up the concrete village road. It is uphill the whole way and the sun is strong; it usually takes
1–1.5 hours
to reach Mongoto Elementary School. Many reports say to keep left at the fork, but confirm with residents.
Near the school, check whether visitor registration is required, and arrange registration and a guide if so. If no one is on hand, ask ahead at the tourism office next to the Atok municipal hall.
From the school, pass along the mountainside road and between the vegetable fields to the three-cross hill and the summit. Sources differ on the time from the school to the top, about
30 minutes–1.5 hours
, and it takes longer if you lose the way.
Enjoy the view near the summit, have lunch, then head back down the way you came. The descent is usually shorter than the climb.
Reach KM 55 and wait for a bus toward Baguio. Plan to arrive well before the last bus.
If you walk, allow about 4–6 hours round trip from the highway entrance to the summit and back.

items.title: Short trip by vehicle
items.subtitle: Drive up the village road and walk a little

children.text: Leave Baguio toward Atok. A van or small car takes around
2–2.5 hours
Ask about registration and a guide at the tourism office next to the Atok municipal hall, and get any needed guidance.
Head up the village road from KM 55. It is narrow and very steep, and large vehicles may not make it, so use a local vehicle or leave yours by the highway and walk.
Drive up as far as you can, then follow the Way of the Cross to the summit on foot, about
15–40 minutes
After the views at the top, come back down and visit the flower farms in Atok and the former highest highway point viewpoint.
Whether you can drive up and how far may change with road conditions and rules, so confirm with local staff first.
Travel from Baguio to Atok, pick a nearby homestay or campsite, and have an early dinner. After sunset it gets close to freezing, so prepare warm clothing.
Wake up, switch on your headlamp and climb with a guide. Always follow your guide's instructions so you do not trample the fields, and avoid climbing alone in the dark.
Watch the sunrise and sea of clouds from the summit. On days with low cloud, the view can be blocked.
Come down, have breakfast, visit sights in Atok such as the Northern Blossom Flower Farm, then return to Baguio.
Buses to Baguio, such as Victory Liner, run all day from the Pasay, Cubao and Sampaloc terminals in Manila. The trip takes about
5–6 hours
on an overnight run, and reports gave fares of about
, but check the latest fare with the operator.
Overnight buses tend to arrive in Baguio around dawn, so you can start hiking the same day you arrive.
Use Manila's international airport (MNL); flights to Baguio's Loakan Airport are limited, so check the schedule.

items.title: From Baguio to the KM 55 entrance

children.text: Take a bus toward Sagada, Bontoc, Buguias or Abatan from the Dangwa bus terminal or the Slaughterhouse terminal on Magsaysay Avenue. Reports mention Rising Sun and Lizardo; tell the conductor "KM 55, Timbak" so they drop you off.
The ride takes
2–3 hours
or more in reports, and fares were about
in reports from 2012 to 2020. The stop is a roadside waiting shed on the right side of the road, marked with a sign.
Buses are infrequent and the last one leaves early, so for a day trip take the first bus and check the return buses in advance.

items.title: Getting around on the village road

children.text: From KM 55 to Mongoto Elementary School, you walk the concrete village road, which usually takes
1–1.5 hours
. It is steep and narrow, and large vehicles have trouble getting up.
You can also rent a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) or a local vehicle to go higher up, but confirm the fare locally.

Some reports say you can climb Mt. Timbak from the Kabayan side by starting in town and walking the opposite route with a local guide. Older records mention a few daily buses from the Baguio Slaughterhouse terminal to Kabayan, but confirm departure times locally.

November through March is the dry season, with good road conditions and many clear days. From December to February, dawn and night temperatures drop to single digits and it is very cold, but the sea of clouds forms best. In the cold season, Atok can drop to around
, and frost sometimes forms.

In the rainy season from June to October, rain and typhoons make the village road slippery and cloudy, and landslides can block Halsema Highway. Some reports mention smoke from wildfires in the late dry season from March to May. During Holy Week, the Way of the Cross processions can bring crowds.

The hike itself fits comfortably in a day, but to see the sunrise it is better to stay at a homestay or campsite around Atok. One 2019 report recorded staying at a local home for about ₱100–350 per person (living room ₱200, bedroom ₱350, tent ₱100), but this figure is confirmed by only one report and may have changed, so check directly with the host when booking. Homestays and transient houses in Atok town (Sayangan) were listed at about ₱600–1,200 per night in a 2025 article (unclear whether per person or per room). If you want lodging closer to the city, the easiest option is to stay in Baguio and take the first bus in the morning.

There are no restaurants on the trail, only a few small stores, so bring water, snacks and a packed lunch. On the way back, you can enjoy vegetables, coffee and flower-farm snacks around Atok or Sayangan. This is a place where people live, so please carry all your trash back down.
If you walk up the village road from KM 55, take the first bus and start early. The sun is strong at midday and the last bus leaves early.
Reported times to the summit range from 15 minutes to 2 hours. It depends on how far you ride, so leave some slack in your schedule.

If you are unsure of the way, ask residents at roadside houses or small stores. Many reports say people hiked without a guide, but registration and guide requirements have varied over time, so confirm locally.
You need a thick jacket, gloves and a hat at dawn, and sunscreen and sunglasses by day. It can feel like the seasons change within a single day.

The fields are the residents' livelihood. Do not step on or pick the crops; walk only on the concrete road and field-edge paths. Some reports say that with a guide you may get permission to use shortcuts.
The mountain is sacred to the Ibaloi people, and records say access to the summit can be closed during a burial. Follow the signs and what local residents tell you.
The concrete road is very steep, so wear non-slip sneakers or hiking boots and consider bringing knee supports or trekking poles.
It is worthwhile to combine a flower farm in Atok and the former highest highway point in the same plan.

Visits to the Timbak cave and its mummies are reported to be suspended for conservation, so do not come to see the mummies, and because the whole mountain is residents' farmland and burial ground, follow local rules. Check the latest notice at the Atok tourism office for registration and guide requirements and fees.
At nearly 2,700 m, you may get short of breath and some people feel mild altitude symptoms. Walk slowly and drink plenty of water.
The village road from KM 55 is very steep and narrow, large vehicles such as vans may not be able to climb it, and it is more dangerous in the rain.
When fog or cloud rolls in, everything turns white and it is easy to lose the way. Plan to be down before sunset.
Wildfires sometimes break out in the late dry season and smoke can linger. Be careful not to leave any embers behind.
The last bus leaves early, so check the return buses in advance; if you miss it, you have to flag down a van on the highway or stay overnight in Atok.
The town the mountain belongs to, with the Northern Blossom Flower Farm and the former highest highway point, about
10–15 minutes
by car from the KM 55 entrance.
A burial-culture site of the Ibaloi on the other side of the mountain. The Timbak cave is reported to be closed to visits, so check the latest situation.
Luzon's second-highest peak, visible in the distance from the summit and climbed as a separate trip.
The starting city, with bus terminals, lodging and restaurants.
